sections.html:
The reason for the move decides the paper. Unpaid rent calls for a three day demand, a broken lease term calls for a seven day letter, and a tenancy with no fixed end calls for a longer heads-up tied to the rental period.

Chapter 83 of the Florida Statutes, the residential landlord and tenant chapter, holds every one of these clocks. A landlord who serves the wrong form, or counts days loosely, hands the tenant a ready defense before the case is even filed.

Owners with a house to sell have extra reason to get this right. Buyers ask early whether the property will be empty at closing, and the honest answer depends on a valid notice.

Section 83.56(3) has the landlord deliver a written demand for the rent or for possession of the home. The tenant then has three days, and the count skips Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays.

So a demand delivered on a Friday doesn't expire the following Monday. Landlords who count every calendar day often file too soon, and a case filed too soon is a weak case.

  • The demand must ask for payment or for the unit back.
  • It must be written, and no lease term can excuse the landlord from serving it.
  • Rent taken after the demand needs a receipt showing the balance owed, a deposit of the partial amount with the court registry at filing, or a brand new demand.

That last item trips up small owners. Cashing a half payment and then suing on the old demand can sink the case.

sections.h2: What if the tenant breaks the lease but rent is current?
sections.html:
The statute sorts breaches into two kinds. If the tenant can fix the problem, the notice gives seven days after delivery to do so. If the problem can't be fixed, such as intentional damage or an ongoing unreasonable disturbance, the notice gives seven days to move out.

A repeat of the same breach inside twelve months lets the landlord go to court without serving another notice, so keep old notices on file.

The letter should say exactly what the tenant did and what must change. A loose, general complaint gives the tenant room to claim the instructions were unclear.

The section allows mailing, handing the tenant a true copy, emailing under section 83.505, or leaving a copy at the home if the tenant is absent. Whichever way you choose, record it.

Lease language can't take away these requirements. A clause that has the tenant give up notice, or trims the number of days, carries no weight under the statute. Still read the lease, since it may name the place for notices or the rent amount.

  • Date the paper and make a copy for the file.
  • Write down the name of the person who delivered it and the hour.
  • Mark the last day of the count on a calendar, leaving out weekends and legal holidays for the rent demand.

When a rental has no set end date, section 83.57 ties the warning to the rental period, and the notice has to arrive before that period closes.

Warning needed to end a periodic Florida tenancy under section 83.57
Kind of tenancyMinimum warning
Year to year60 days
Quarter to quarter30 days
Month to month30 days
Week to week7 days

Single family rentals are usually month to month once the first lease year ends. An owner planning to list the house can use this path when the tenant is in good standing, as long as the paper goes out early enough for the period to end on time.

A short paper trail protects a notice that gets challenged. The file should show what went out, who received it, how it was delivered, and the day the count began.

  • A copy of the notice exactly as served, with the rental address.
  • Proof of delivery: a mail receipt, a note from the person who handed it over, or the email record.
  • A rent ledger showing the balance on the day of service.
  • Any receipt given for partial rent taken later.

Title agents reviewing an occupied rental sale like to see these papers, since they show nothing was left half done.

sections.h2: Mistakes that sink an eviction notice
sections.html:
Most notices fail on details, and a checklist catches them.

  • Counting Saturdays, Sundays or court observed legal holidays in the three day rent demand.
  • Demanding more than the tenant owes, or leaving out whether the landlord wants rent or the keys.
  • Mixing a rent demand with a lease breach on one confusing page.
  • Giving a curable breach only a vacate deadline, with no chance to fix it.
  • Taking rent after the demand without a receipt, a registry deposit or a fresh demand.
  • Serving a periodic tenancy notice too late for the rental period to end when planned.

A defective notice usually means starting over, which costs days. When a sale date is on the calendar, those days can cost more than the original rent problem. Draft the paper against the statute section that fits.

Tenants who receive any notice should read it for the stated reason and the number of days, and keep proof of payments. The clerk of the county court can explain how a case is filed, though the clerk can't give legal advice.

sections.h2: What follows once the notice runs out?
sections.html:
The landlord files in county court. Removing a tenant who stays belongs to the sheriff, and a landlord who locks the door or hauls out belongings without a court order is outside the process.

A tenant who answers with any defense besides payment has five days after service, again skipping weekends and legal holidays, to put the accrued rent in the court registry or ask the court to set it. Miss that and the defenses are waived, which allows a prompt default judgment under section 83.60(2).

After judgment the clerk sends a writ to the sheriff, who posts it and waits 24 hours before returning the home to the landlord. Weekends and holidays don't pause that day under section 83.62.

A rented home can be sold, but the notice period and the court calendar decide when a buyer gets keys. Owners who need a firm closing date should choose early between selling with the tenant in place and delivering the house empty.

  • Sell with the tenant in place and pass the lease to the buyer.
  • End a periodic tenancy with the proper warning, then list the home vacant.
  • Serve a rent or breach notice if the tenant is in default and wait out the court steps.

Every route starts with a valid notice. Lenders and title agents may hold up a closing while an occupant remains. For advice on a specific notice, talk to a Florida attorney or the clerk of the county court where the home sits.

faqs.q: How many days is the Florida notice for unpaid rent?
faqs.a: Three days, with Saturdays, Sundays and court observed legal holidays left out of the count. The written demand must ask for the rent or for possession.

faqs.q: Can a Florida landlord skip the notice?
faqs.a: No. A missing or defective notice gives the tenant a defense, and the lease can't waive the requirement.

faqs.q: How much notice ends a month to month tenancy in Florida?
faqs.a: At least 30 days before the monthly period ends. Year to year tenancies need 60 days, and week to week tenancies need 7.

faqs.q: What if the tenant breaks a lease term but pays rent?
faqs.a: The landlord serves a seven day notice. A curable breach gets seven days to cure, and one that can't be cured gets seven days to vacate.

faqs.q: Who removes a tenant after the landlord wins in court?
faqs.a: The sheriff. The clerk issues a writ, and the sheriff posts a 24 hour notice before putting the landlord in possession.
